title: Using ChatGPT for Science Learning: A Study on Pre-service Teachers' Lesson Planning

01_initial_request.target_name: empirical characterization of how 29 Korean pre-service elementary science teachers integrated ChatGPT into elementary science lesson plans
01_initial_request.input_data: 29 ChatGPT-integrated science lesson plans, attached simulated teacher/student-ChatGPT conversations, and open-ended survey responses from 29 pre-service elementary science teachers at a Korean teachers' university; participants included 11 males and 18 females, mostly sophomores, after a 3-week on-site teacher training experience and four 2-hour course sessions in May-June 2023; resources included the Korean national curriculum and elementary science textbooks
01_initial_request.user_intent: to address the lack of empirical studies on practical ChatGPT integration in science education, especially evidence about its applicable range across science domains and teaching strategies, pre-service teachers' TPACK-like proficiency, and their perceived usefulness and concerns
01_initial_request.quantifiable_goal: analyze all 29 lesson plans; classify science domains and teaching/learning strategies; evaluate plans with a modified 4-item TIAR/TPACK-based rubric on a 1-4 scale; compare rubric item scores statistically; summarize survey themes by participant counts out of N=29

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Prior literature proposed ChatGPT and other large-language models as promising tools for education, including automatic assessment, grading, learning guidance, and science inquiry support. [Gap] Most work as of August 2023 was visionary or presumptive, with few empirical studies of actual ChatGPT integration into science teaching and learning or teachers' perceptions. [Decision] The authors framed three research questions targeting applicable range, proficiency of integration, and perceived usefulness/concerns in pre-service teachers' science lesson plans.

parameters.research_questions: RQ1 applicable range of integrating ChatGPT into science lesson plans; RQ2 proficiency in planning and integrating ChatGPT; RQ3 perceived usefulness and concerns
parameters.time_context: ChatGPT released November 2022; study conducted May-June 2023

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The study was positioned around a concrete empirical gap: lack of evidence on how ChatGPT can be used across science content domains and teaching/learning methods in lesson planning.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] The participants were pre-service elementary teachers who had prior exposure to the Korean 2015 Revised National Curriculum and had completed a 3-week school-based teacher-training experience. [Gap] Most participants were unfamiliar with ChatGPT or LLMs before the study, so they needed a common baseline for lesson planning with ChatGPT. [Decision] The instructor delivered four structured 2-hour sessions to introduce ChatGPT, discuss its benefits, review science teaching methods, and support lesson-plan writing.

parameters.session_topics: ChatGPT fundamentals; potential benefits in science teaching/learning; science teaching methods including learning cycle, POE, discovery learning, analogy generation, concept mapping, epistemological vee, and role-playing; lesson-plan crafting with instructor feedback

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Participants received a common introduction to ChatGPT and science teaching strategies before producing lesson plans.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Lesson-plan analysis can reveal teachers' content, pedagogical, and technological knowledge, and the study needed artifacts showing actual planned ChatGPT use. [Gap] General opinions alone would not show how ChatGPT was embedded into concrete learning activities. [Decision] The authors required each participant to draft a 45-minute elementary science lesson plan using at least one teaching/learning method and at least one teacher or student query to ChatGPT, plus an attached simulated ChatGPT conversation and survey responses.

parameters.required_ChatGPT_use: at least one teacher or student query to ChatGPT, with the lesson structured around ChatGPT responses
parameters.required_attachment: simulated conversation with ChatGPT aligned with the lesson plan
parameters.survey_questions: rationale for content/method selection; why ChatGPT integration was beneficial; anticipated outcomes for science education
parameters.provided_resources: national curriculum and elementary school science textbooks

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The corpus consisted of 29 lesson plans, associated simulated ChatGPT interactions, and survey responses suitable for rubric scoring, descriptive classification, and qualitative analysis.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Harris et al.'s Technology Integration Assessment Rubric measures the quality of technology integration through TPACK-related criteria. [Gap] The original rubric referred to technology broadly, while this study focused specifically on ChatGPT and its response-generating functions. [Decision] The authors modified TIAR by replacing technology with ChatGPT and revising the technology-selection item into ChatGPT function selection.

tool.name: modified TPACK-based Technology Integration Assessment Rubric
tool.version: revised from Harris et al. TIAR

parameters.criteria: curriculum goals & ChatGPT; instructional methods/strategies & ChatGPT; ChatGPT function selection(s); fit
parameters.reliability_estimate: Cronbach's alpha = .69 for 4 items across 29 lesson-plan evaluations

02_agent_trajectory.observation: A ChatGPT-specific 4-item rubric was created; its internal consistency was reported as acceptable with Cronbach's alpha of .69.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] The lesson plans and surveys required both structured scoring and interpretation of open-ended responses. [Gap] Single-pass coding could miss discrepancies and emergent themes in teachers' rationales and concerns. [Decision] Two researchers coded lesson plans and survey responses, resolved discrepancies through iterative discussion, used the constant comparative method for categories, and triangulated with the attached ChatGPT conversation data.

tool.name: constant comparative method and TIAR coding

parameters.independent_coding: two researchers independently coded 10 and 9 science lesson plans respectively based on TIAR and survey responses
parameters.triangulation_source: simulated chat data between participants and ChatGPT

02_agent_trajectory.observation: The authors generated rubric scores and qualitative categories while checking interpretations against lesson-plan and simulated-chat evidence.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] RQ1 asked how broadly ChatGPT could be integrated across science domains and instructional methods. [Gap] The authors needed to quantify which content areas and strategies appeared in the 29 plans. [Decision] They descriptively coded target science domains and teaching/learning methods or strategies in each lesson plan.

tool.name: descriptive frequency analysis of lesson-plan categories

parameters.domain_categories: biology, chemistry, earth science, physics, environmental science
parameters.method_categories_reported: cooperative learning, POE, learning cycle, analogy generation, experimentation, concept mapping, and others

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Target domains were biology 9/29, chemistry 7/29, earth science 7/29, physics 4/29, and environmental science 4/29, with multiple domains allowed. Common instructional strategies were cooperative learning 7/29, POE 6/29, learning cycle 6/29, analogy generation 4/29, experimentation 3/29, and concept mapping 3/29.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] RQ2 required evaluating how proficiently pre-service teachers integrated ChatGPT, not just whether they used it. [Gap] The authors needed to identify strengths and weaknesses across curriculum alignment, instructional strategy support, function selection, and overall fit. [Decision] They scored each plan with the modified TIAR rubric and compared item means using paired-samples t-tests.

tool.name: modified TIAR scoring and paired-samples t-test

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Overall TIAR score was M=3.29, SD=.91. Item means were curriculum goals & ChatGPT M=3.44, SD=.87; instructional methods/strategies & ChatGPT M=3.48, SD=.99; ChatGPT function selection(s) M=3.00, SD=.93; fit M=3.24, SD=.83. The only significant item difference reported was between item 2 and item 3, t(28)=2.3173, p=.0280, indicating stronger integration into instructional strategies than selection of ChatGPT functions.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Rubric scores showed generally high integration quality but lower performance on ChatGPT function selection. [Gap] The authors needed to interpret what counted as appropriate or inappropriate ChatGPT use and understand teachers' perceived benefits and risks. [Decision] They examined example lesson plans and open-ended survey themes, including both positive affordances and concerns.

tool.name: qualitative thematic analysis of lesson plans and survey responses

parameters.theme_counting: number of participants agreeing with each theme

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Appropriate uses included Participant_7 using ChatGPT as a complementary information source in Jigsaw expert groups, Participant_11 using it for role-play organization and feedback on ecological-balance scripts, and Participant_20 using consecutive questioning within cooperative learning. Inappropriate or risky uses included Participant_3 asking ChatGPT for constellation positions despite the visual nature of the task, Participant_20 using ChatGPT-suggested YouTube links that were non-existent and not checked, and Participant_8 using ChatGPT to design acids-and-bases experiments in a way that could undermine inquiry skills. Survey themes included knowledge construction through questioning 16/29, individualized learning support 9/29, formative assessment 8/29, digital competency/literacy 4/29, accuracy/reliability/security concerns 11/29, and over-dependence concerns 13/29.

02_agent_trajectory.thought: [Background] Teachers' concerns about accuracy and over-dependence were prominent, and example cases showed hallucinated links and potentially excessive delegation to ChatGPT. [Gap] The study needed practical mitigation ideas for classroom dynamics around ChatGPT. [Decision] The authors summarized participants' suggested safeguards before, during, and after ChatGPT use.

parameters.information_sources_to_reduce_overdepend: self 2, peer 1, teacher 3, experiment 1, ChatGPT 2, unspecified 1
parameters.before_using_ChatGPT: teach characteristics and possible pitfalls of ChatGPT, 6 participants
parameters.during_using_ChatGPT: structure learning so students use ChatGPT limitedly and have time to interact with peers and teacher, 6 participants
parameters.after_using_ChatGPT: verify ChatGPT-provided information with students, 8 participants

02_agent_trajectory.observation: Participants proposed a more systematic classroom process: teach ChatGPT's limitations, limit its use within peer/teacher interaction, and verify information after use.

03_success_verification.validation_technique: The authors verified their claims through analysis of 29 lesson plans using a modified 4-item TPACK/TIAR rubric, descriptive frequency counts of science domains and teaching strategies, paired-samples t-test comparison of rubric item scores, qualitative constant-comparative analysis of survey responses, and triangulation with simulated ChatGPT conversation attachments.

overall_TPAR_TIA_rubric_score.interpretation: average lesson-plan quality exceeded the 2.5 midpoint, supporting the claim that pre-service teachers showed reasonably high competence in integrating ChatGPT

curriculum_goals_and_ChatGPT.interpretation: ChatGPT use was generally aligned with science curriculum goals

instructional_methods_strategies_and_Cha.interpretation: highest-scoring dimension, indicating ChatGPT was often well matched with instructional strategies

ChatGPT_function_selection.interpretation: lowest-scoring dimension, showing that selecting appropriate ChatGPT functions remained a relative weakness

fit_score.interpretation: content, pedagogy, and ChatGPT function generally fit together, though not as strongly as the best individual dimensions

item2_vs_item3_t_test.interpretation: instructional-strategy integration scored significantly higher than ChatGPT function selection at p<.05

rubric_internal_consistency.interpretation: reported as within the acceptable range for the four modified TIAR items

domain_coverage.value: biology 9/29; chemistry 7/29; earth science 7/29; physics 4/29; environmental science 4/29
domain_coverage.interpretation: ChatGPT was applied across multiple elementary science domains, with multiple-domain coding allowed

concern_overdependence.interpretation: student over-dependence on ChatGPT was the most frequently reported concern

concern_accuracy_reliability_security.interpretation: a substantial subset of teachers worried about ChatGPT's accuracy, reliability, and security

03_success_verification.final_verdict: The study met its empirical goal of characterizing 29 pre-service teachers' ChatGPT-integrated science lesson plans. The results showed broad but uneven applicability across science domains and teaching strategies, with an overall modified TIAR score of 3.29/4 indicating reasonably strong integration. However, the goal was only partially met with respect to demonstrating high-quality function selection: the ChatGPT function-selection item was the lowest-scoring dimension at 3.00/4 and was significantly lower than instructional-strategy integration, revealing concrete limitations and misuse cases.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: ChatGPT function selection was weaker than integration with instructional strategies.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The item 'ChatGPT function selection(s)' averaged 3.00, lower than 'instructional methods/strategies & ChatGPT' at 3.48, with a significant paired-samples t-test difference, t(28)=2.3173, p=.0280. The authors attributed this to a mix of suitable and unsuitable ChatGPT applications in the lesson plans.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors highlighted appropriate function-selection examples and argued that teachers need better support in exploiting ChatGPT's functions according to curriculum goals and instructional strategies.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: A lesson plan asked students to use ChatGPT for locating constellations in the night sky.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The task was visual in nature, whereas ChatGPT as used in May 2023 did not afford much visual information, making it poorly suited for that activity.
04_failure_modes.correction: The paper identified this as an inappropriate use case; future lesson design should match ChatGPT to language- and dialogue-suitable tasks or use other visual/astronomical resources for constellation-position activities.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: A participant used ChatGPT to recommend YouTube video links and submitted ChatGPT-generated summaries of videos that did not exist.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The YouTube links provided by ChatGPT were non-existent, and the participant did not check whether they existed, illustrating reliability and hallucination problems.
04_failure_modes.correction: Participants and teachers should verify ChatGPT-provided information and links; 8 participants specifically suggested verifying ChatGPT-provided information with students after use.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: A lesson plan proposed that student groups use ChatGPT to design acids-and-bases experiments.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: The authors warned that this use requires caution because it could undermine students' practical inquiry skills over time if ChatGPT substitutes for students' own experimental reasoning.
04_failure_modes.correction: The authors suggested systematic classroom structuring to limit over-dependence, including having students think first, interact with peers and teachers, and use ChatGPT only in constrained ways.

04_failure_modes.what_failed: Pre-service teachers anticipated student over-dependence on ChatGPT and concerns about accuracy, reliability, and security.
04_failure_modes.diagnosis: Survey responses showed over-dependence concerns from 13/29 participants and accuracy/reliability/security concerns from 11/29 participants, consistent with observed inappropriate use cases.
04_failure_modes.correction: Suggested mitigations included teaching ChatGPT's characteristics and pitfalls before use, limiting ChatGPT use during learning while preserving peer/teacher interaction, and verifying ChatGPT-provided information after use.
